newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN yearbook offers weird and wonderful data.
newsitem.headline: UN yearbook offers weird and wonderful data.

text.p: The British are less likely to die from traffic accidents than anyone else in Europe or North America but have some of the highest cancer death rates, while Scandinavians, Austrians and Swiss are the most likely to kill themselves.
More couples stay in wedlock in the Mediterranean countries of Italy, Turkey and Greece while the rate of divorce is highest in Estonia, Latvia, Belgium, Sweden, Finland, Russia and Britain.
The Swiss have the highest proportion of computer-users along with the United States and Denmark, while the Finns have the highest proportion of "surfers" on the Internet computer network.
These and many off-beat snippets of information are revealed in the latest annual reference book of the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (ECE), unveiled on Tuesday.

Culled from data provided by the Geneva-based agency's 55 member countries, ranging from North America and Europe to the former Soviet republics, the report aims to give a detailed economic and social picture of the region.
"Trends in Europe and North America" found Tajikistan the poorest country in the northern hemisphere with a per capita income of just $103 a year.
Luxembourg was the richest with a per capita income of more than $30,000, followed by the United States with $26,500 and Switzerland with $24,400.
The number of television sets per head of population was the highest in Britain and Monaco while only 89 people in a thousand had one in Albania.
Finnish households are the loneliest in the region with nearly half made up of just one person while Israel boasts the most crowded ones, the report said.
The average home in Switzerland also had just two people living in it, compared to more than five in the Moslem Transcaucasian republic of Azerbaijan.
The women of Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan in Central Asia were among the most fertile with birth rates of 145 and 149 per 1,000 -- three times higher than many west European countries.
The study found fertility rates the lowest in Russia, Slovenia, Spain in Italy with between 36 and 38 births per 1,000 women.
It said birth rates in the region had been declining since the last report, published in 1995, except in Denmark, Finland, Luxembourg and the United States, where they had risen slightly.
The United States also had the highest rate of teenage mothers in Western countries covered by the report, with 13 percent.
The proportion of young mothers was the highest in Bulgaria, where women under 20 years of age accounted for 23 percent of all births.
The women of Switzerland and the Netherlands had some of the lowest rates of extramarital births, and Iceland and Sweden some of the highest.
There were nearly two abortions for every child born in Russia, where abortions are used as a birth control method, and just one per 1,000 births in staunchly Catholic Poland.

Houses in the United States were the most spacious with nearly half having six rooms or more. In the Czech Republic, the average one-family apartment or house was 40 square metres and had fewer than three rooms.
Half the homes in former Soviet Kazakhstan had no piped water, bathroom or flushing toilets.
